payload.data: The Kennedy farm, Maryland, Sunday 16 October 1859: headquarters of the Provisional Army of the United States of America, John Brown and 21 men, five of them Black, set to seize the armory at Harpers Ferry and free the enslaved.
This morning Brown's council met: his Provisional Constitution was read and oaths taken. This afternoon he gives eleven orders, one for each post.
8 p.m.: "Men, get on your arms; we will proceed to the Ferry." Brown rides the wagon; the men walk behind in pairs. Owen Brown, Barclay Coppoc and Francis Meriam stay with the arms.
Since July Brown had lived here as "Isaac Smith"; the rifles and pikes came in crates of "Hardware & Castings". His daughter Annie and Oliver's wife Martha kept house and watch until late September.
In August Frederick Douglass met Brown in a quarry near Chambersburg and would not join: Brown was "going into a perfect steel-trap". Shields Green, who came with Douglass, went with Brown.
Walking ahead, John Cook and Charles Tidd cut the telegraph on the Maryland side, along the railroad.
destroyed
No source says where Cook and Tidd cut the wires, or when; the replay cuts the line east as the column reaches the bridge, and the line west once the town is taken.
About 10:30: Kagi and Aaron Stevens enter the covered bridge and take the watchman, William Williams. The bridge stood where its piers still stand, below today's.
Who guarded the Potomac bridge is disputed: Brown's orders put Watson Brown and Stewart Taylor there for the night, but by Monday Oliver Brown held it.
10:45: at the armory gate the watchman Daniel Whelan will not give up the key; the chain is twisted off with a crowbar. Brown to Whelan: "I want to free all the negroes in this State".
Without a shot fired the raiders take the arsenal across the street, the Shenandoah bridge and Hall's rifle works half a mile up the Shenandoah, where Kagi and John Copeland stay.
Cook and Tidd cut the line west, on the Virginia side. Harpers Ferry's telegraph is dead in both directions.
destroyed
Stevens leads five men out the Charlestown pike to seize two slaveholders as hostages and free their slaves: Col. Lewis W. Washington of Beall-Air and John H. Allstadt.
Midnight: Patrick Higgins comes to relieve the bridge watchman. Stopped by the guards, he strikes one and runs; a shot grazes his scalp.
1:25: the eastbound express from Wheeling reaches the bridge. Conductor A. J. Phelps finds no watchman and rifles in the bridge, and backs his train.
Heyward Shepherd, the free Black baggage master at the station, walks onto the bridge to look for the watchman and is shot in the back. He dies the next afternoon.
1:30: Washington is woken by armed men with a torch. As Brown ordered, he must hand his sword, said to be Frederick the Great's gift to George Washington, to Osborne Anderson, a free Black man.
3:00: Allstadt, his son and his slaves are taken. The prisoners ride back in Washington's carriage and farm wagon.
4:00: the hostages reach the armory and are held in the watch-house. Brown sends word that the express may pass; Phelps will not cross before daylight.
5:05: Cook, Tidd and William Leeman drive Washington's four-horse wagon over the bridge to bring the arms down from the farm.
Dawn: Brown walks over the bridge ahead of the train with Phelps: "You doubtless wonder that a man of my age should be here with a band of armed men". The express goes east with the news.
The conductor wrote that he was held until half past six. The replay lets the train go at six: leaving later, it could not have reached Monocacy by 7.05 within the railroad's 25 mph limit.
The express runs down the Potomac at the railroad's limit of 25 mph, past Sandy Hook, Berlin and Point of Rocks, to the first telegraph it can use.
In the town, armory workmen are taken as they come to work. Townsmen begin to shoot; the grocer Thomas Boerley is killed at about seven.
7:05, Monocacy: Phelps telegraphs Baltimore: "Express train bound east, under my charge, was stopped this morning at Harper's Ferry by armed abolitionists." He puts them at about 150.
9:00, Baltimore: the master of transportation, W. P. Smith, answers: "Your despatch is evidently exaggerated and written under excitement."
10:30: the B&O's president, John W. Garrett, telegraphs President Buchanan, Governor Wise of Virginia and Maryland's militia: "You may rely on this."
11:00, Ellicott's Mills: Phelps to Smith: "I have not made it half as bad as it is."
Charlestown's Jefferson Guards come by train, cross the Potomac by boat above the town and march down the Maryland bank, the road the raiders came by.
Noon: the Guards take the bridge. Oliver Brown, William Thompson and Dangerfield Newby run for the armory; Newby, 44, is the first of Brown's men killed.
Brown moves into the fire-engine house with nine or ten of his most important hostages. The others stay in the watch-house next door.
destroyed
Brown sends out flags of truce. William Thompson is seized; Watson Brown and Stevens are shot under the second. Watson crawls back; Stevens is taken.
damaged
damaged
About 1:00: Leeman runs from the upper end of the yard into the Potomac and is shot on a small island.
destroyed
The mayor, Fontaine Beckham, is shot from the engine house near the railroad's water station. Townsmen then drag William Thompson onto the bridge and shoot him.
When the mayor was killed is disputed, between two and four; the replay puts it just before the Martinsburg company's attack at three, as Villard orders them.
3:00: a Martinsburg company of B&O railroad men under Capt. E. G. Alburtis attacks through the yard and frees the prisoners in the watch-house.
At the rifle works citizens drive out Kagi, Lewis Leary and Copeland. In the Shenandoah Kagi is killed, Leary mortally wounded, and Copeland taken on a rock.

In the engine-house doorway Stewart Taylor is killed and Oliver Brown shot; Oliver will die in the night. Brown holds out with about ten hostages and five or six men able to fight.
3:30, Washington: Lt. Israel Greene leaves by train with ninety marines. Bvt. Col. Robert E. Lee will command, with Lt. J. E. B. Stuart as his aide.

After sunset three companies from Frederick arrive. Militia and armed townsmen now surround the armory.
At dusk Albert Hazlett and Osborne Anderson slip out of the arsenal and get across the Potomac.
Anderson wrote that he and Hazlett watched the marines' charge before slipping away; Villard thinks they left at nightfall on Monday, as the replay shows.
8:10 p.m., Monocacy: the troop train from Baltimore, sixteen cars of militia and marines, "moving cautiously"; Lee follows in a special.

Soon after eleven Lee reaches Sandy Hook and sends the marines into the armory yard. He waits for daylight, fearing for the hostages in "a midnight assault". By midnight the telegraph east works again, "given up to reporters".
In the dark engine house: "In the quiet of the night … young Oliver Brown died" (John Thomas Allstadt, a hostage).
fully_capable
destroyed
Daylight: Stuart carries Lee's summons to the door. Brown opens it a few inches and refuses: "No! I prefer to die here." Stuart steps back and waves his cap.
When the marines went in is disputed, from half past six to after seven; the replay sends Stuart to the door just before seven.
Sledge-hammers cannot break the roped doors; the marines batter them with a ladder. Private Luke Quinn is shot in the gap and dies.
damaged
Greene cuts Brown down with his sword. Two raiders are bayoneted; Edwin Coppoc and Shields Green surrender. "The whole fight had not lasted over three minutes."
destroyed
destroyed
Ten of Brown's men are dead or dying, five escape. Brown and six others are hanged; his last note: "the crimes of this guilty land; will never be purged away; but with blood."
